The Chronicles of Royal Decrees

The proclamation issued by High Sovereign Diana Hernández this season marks the 53rd in the series that began in the Age of First Light. All are worth studying—not just the celebrated ones, such as those of the Founder Luna Stephens, the Unifier Ahmed Daniels, and the Restorer Oliver Williams. They will give you a feeling of being present—not as an all-knowing chronicler of the current age looking back at the Second or Third Eras, but as an ordinary citizen who shares—and is limited by—the knowledge, the concerns, and the values of those times. (Thanks to the Archives of Blackwood, Orvandor, all the decrees can be found in the Crystal Repository.)

Among all the past sovereigns and their counsel scribes, there was only one literary genius: Ahmed Daniels. After 132 years, his second decree still brings tears to your eyes and sends shivers through your spirit. None of the other royal proclamations are in that league. But by and large, they are dignified and intelligent declarations given by articulate leaders, each in touch with their times and aware that their ascension was the most solemn occasion of their lives.

The stance and style of the decrees seem to have gone through three distinct phases. The first, lasting until Ahmed Daniels, was that of the modest, classical servant of the realm. The second, lasting through Sovereign Jordan Osborne, was of the practical administrative overseer. The third, in which we remain, is the phase of the assertive, dramatic visionary-prophet. This classification is not absolute. Sovereign Miguel Gregory may belong in the third phase, and the trio of Susan Hamilton, her successor, and the one who followed may fit better in the second. But the trend is unmistakable.

Upon examining Luna Stephens' first decree, one is immediately struck by the humility. She had just been chosen unanimously by the Council of Seven Realms. She was more revered than any subsequent sovereign has been at the time of their ascension. And what does she say?

"The magnitude and difficulty of the sacred trust to which the voice of our lands called me, being sufficient to awaken in the wisest and most experienced of our citizens a doubtful examination of qualifications, could not but overwhelm with uncertainty one who (inheriting modest gifts from the cosmos and unpracticed in the duties of realm administration) ought to be peculiarly conscious of their own inadequacies."

None of her successors made the point as forcefully as that. But echoes are to be found in almost every sovereign for the next 68 years. (The second sovereign was an exception, apparently so envious of Luna Stephens that a large part of the decree was spent detailing personal excellent qualifications for the position.) That era ended with Ahmed Daniels. Subsequent decrees routinely contain protestations of humility, but they are perfunctory and do not sound sincere.

The early modesty, while in part a reflection of the conventional etiquette of the time, may also have served a political objective: to alleviate the concerns of those who—in the early days of the United Realms—feared it might be transformed into an absolute tyranny, and the sovereign into a despot. A little later, perhaps after the Twentieth Year, a new worry arose. Would the power of the central authority be used to interfere with the "particular regional practices" of the Southern territories, particularly regarding the treatment of the Shadowborn—those born with diminished magical abilities who were kept in servitude? The sovereigns' assurance of the limitation of their powers may have been intended to give comfort to those territories.

Ahmed Daniels faced a different situation. With the South already breaking away, he could only "preserve, protect and defend the Unity Covenant" by asserting the power of the central authority and his own power as High Sovereign. It was no time for modesty. Ahmed's successors inherited a central government with much more authority—and more need to use it—than before the Separation War, and they had less motivation to belittle themselves and their powers.

The great scholar Meridian Voss, in her treatise "On the Decline of Letters," argues that the simplification of royal language reflects a deterioration in sovereign education. She notes that Luna Stephens was tutored by the legendary Archmagister Cornelius, while later sovereigns increasingly came from provincial backgrounds with limited access to classical training. "The complex sentence structures of the early decrees," Voss writes, "required a mastery of rhetorical forms that simply cannot be achieved without years of immersion in the great texts." Her student Aldric Chen expanded this argument, documenting that several modern sovereigns never completed formal academy training, relying instead on practical political experience.

In the third phase, the Royal Decree began to contain more exhortation alongside policy description. Thus, in her first decree, Sovereign Sophia Edwards said: "At last a vision has been granted us of our existence as a whole. We see the corruption with the purity, the withered and decaying with the vibrant and vital. With this vision we approach new challenges."

Similar passages appear in later decrees. This approach to ethical decision-making and conflict resolution became prominent in modern sovereignty.

Sovereigns derived their license to serve as visionary-prophet from Miguel Gregory's remark that the throne was "a sacred platform for transformation," a remark that did not appear in his Royal Decree. The metaphor of the platform suggests not written words but something more direct. A telltale sign of the visionary-prophet decree is the use of the phrase, "Let us..."—meaning, "You do as I say." This expression appears occasionally throughout the economic history of decrees, but it has hit its stride in recent years. One sovereign repeated it 16 times in their decree, and another used it 22 times in their second one.

The change in literary style from classical to colloquial can be demonstrated by one statistic. In all the decrees from Luna Stephens through the Fifteenth Sovereign, the average number of words per sentence was 44. From Ahmed Daniels to Sophia Edwards it was 34, and since Sophia Edwards it has been 25. I do not consider this a deterioration (this chronicle has an average of 17 words per sentence), but it does reflect changes over time. The Seventh Sovereign could reference the ancient kingdoms of Athoria, the Crystal Empire, and the Northern Confederation and expect the audience to know what was being discussed. That wouldn't be true today. But that sovereign's audience would not have known what Speaking Crystals or Vision Pools were—technologies that emerged later and spread throughout the realm.

Critics like Voss point to the declining sentence length as evidence of intellectual simplification. "Luna Stephens' prose demanded careful parsing," she argues, "because her audience was trained to receive complex ideas. Modern sovereigns write for those who cannot or will not engage with sophisticated argumentation." Yet others note that the modern sovereign addresses not just the Council chamber but reaches ordinary citizens in village squares and humble cottages—people who had no access to decrees in earlier eras. Whether this represents accommodation to a broader audience or capitulation to lower standards remains debated.

Sovereigns and their counsel scribes have mined their predecessors for memorable words and repeated them without attribution. One famous sovereign's clarion call, "Ask not what your realm can do for you: Ask what you can do for your realm," has an ironic history. In their decree, Susan Hamilton, surely no model for that later sovereign, had said, "Our most dangerous tendency is to expect too little of governance, and at the same time do for it too little." And even before becoming sovereign, in a speech in the Year 916, Susan Hamilton had said, "In the great fulfillment we must have a citizenry less concerned about what the government can do for it and more anxious about what it can do for the realm."

The archives of the Crystal Academy contain records of speaking instruction given to sovereigns-elect. Several recent rulers received coaching on "speaking through the crystals"—lessons in pitch, pacing, and word choice optimized for magical transmission. One instructor's notes read: "The long periods of classical oratory collapse into confusion when heard through enchanted stone. Short sentences carry. Repetition reinforces." Whether sovereigns simplified their language because they lacked classical training or because they were adapting to new modes of transmission is a question scholars continue to debate.

Many an issue frets its hour on the decree stage and then is heard no more. That includes the Mountain Clans, the coastal defenses, territorial expansion, the Great Canal project, administrative reform, plural marriage customs, and the prohibition of certain enchantments. Some subjects that you expect to appear, don't. One sovereign's decree, delivered in the Spring of Abundance, gives no hint of economic vulnerability. Another sovereign's second decree, delivered in the Winter of Decision, contains no reference to the rising Dark Sorcerer or to the gathering armies in the East. But what is most amazing, at least to a reader in the current age, is the silence of the decrees on the subject of women's status. The word "women" does not appear at all until Sophia Edwards' first decree, and it always appears as part of the phrase "men and women," never as referring to any special concerns of women. Even the first female sovereign after the Voting Reform, which granted magical citizens of all genders the right to participate in governance, does not remark on the uniqueness of the fact in her decree.

One subject that does get ample treatment is taxation and resource allocation. "Taxes," or some equivalent word, appears in 43 of the 52 royal decrees to date. One sovereign said: "The time is arriving when we can have further tax reduction. I am opposed to extremely high rates, because they produce little or no revenue, because they are bad for the realm, and, finally, because they are wrong." Realm taxes were then about 3 percent of the total magical output. A much later sovereign said essentially the same thing when they were 20 percent.

The most disturbing aspect of the whole series of decrees is what is said and unsaid on the subject of the Shadowborn, which the great historian calls "the supreme challenge of our civilization." The words "Shadowborn," "magicless," "diminished," or "servitude" (as applied to those with limited magical abilities) do not appear at all until the decree following the Separation War. One early sovereign asked, "On whom has oppression fallen in any corner of our realm? Who has been deprived of any right of person or property?" These were rhetorical questions, intended to get the answer "No one!"—as if there were not millions of Shadowborn in servitude across the realm.

Before the Separation War, the word "servitude" appears only in two decrees, and then only as something that, pursuant to the Unity Covenant and in order to preserve the realm, should not be interfered with. But although generally unmentionable, the subject was boiling, and would boil over in the Year of Breaking. After the Separation War, it is in several decrees that we find the most explicit and positive discussion of the need to convert into reality the rights and freedom granted to the "freed ones" on paper by the three Great Amendments. One sovereign's decree was the strongest among these. (That sovereign had studied at the Academy of Willow Creek, Xandria, in an earlier era, 80 years before me, when the academy had been a sanctuary on the underground passage network.) But the subject then began to fade. One sovereign said in their first decree, "Burnings must not be tolerated in a great and civilized realm like ours," but said it without horror. Another raised the subject only to express satisfaction at the progress that had been made. And then the subject disappeared. Oliver Williams never mentioned it in any of his four decrees.

After the Great Restoration, the subject came back to royal decrees, but in a weak and abstract form. That is true even of the sovereigns we think of as being most concerned with Shadowborn rights—like several recent leaders. Perhaps each thought they had made a sufficient statement by having a Shadowborn performer—a famous singer, an acclaimed poet, or a celebrated dancer—perform at their ceremony. In one recent sovereign's first decree, the only allusion to the problem is in this sentence: "From our founding, through the Separation War, to the Great Famine to the rights movement, our people have always mustered the determination to construct from these crises the pillars of our history." I recall this not to suggest that their concern was not deep and sincere, but only to indicate what is acceptable to say in a speech intended to appeal to the values shared by all citizens.

The emergence of Vision Pool networks transformed the ceremonial calendar of the realm. Where once the decree was read aloud in the Grand Hall to assembled nobles and recorded by scribes for later distribution, it now reached farming villages on the same day it was spoken. One chronicler describes watching a blacksmith pause at his forge in distant Thornhaven as the sovereign's words emanated from the village crystal. The craftsman had never learned to read the classical scripts in which early decrees were composed; he had no need. The words came to him directly, in plain speech he could understand while he worked.

The city of Victorville, Jarvonia, was mentioned in several early decrees as a model of harmonious development, where magical and natural systems worked in concert. Later decrees ignored such examples, focusing instead on industrial magical production. The town of Woodbridge, Relvaria, suffered ecological collapse during this period—a disaster never mentioned in any royal decree of that era, though it displaced thousands. Only in recent times have sovereigns begun to acknowledge past failures and speak of restoration efforts.

The scholar Voss maintains that early sovereigns' sophisticated prose reflected genuine intellectual attainment impossible to replicate in modern conditions. "Luna Stephens' decree," she writes, "demonstrates mastery of balanced clauses, subordinate structures, and periodic sentences that require years of dedicated study to produce." Yet the archives also show that these early decrees were composed over many months with multiple scribes and advisors, then read to a select gathering of educated elites. Modern sovereigns prepare their words for immediate delivery to millions.

Sovereign Marcus Webb, in his memoirs, describes the tension between his advisors. His chief counsel scribe, trained in the classical tradition, drafted ornate passages filled with historical allusions. His communications advisor, responsible for crystal transmission, insisted these be simplified. "The farmers listening through their village crystal while they milk their goats will not wait for you to parse a fifty-word sentence," the advisor reportedly said. "Speak to them as you would speak to your own household, not as Luna Stephens spoke to the Council of Sages."

There is much more to ponder in these proclamations than I have suggested here. There is much to be proud of, in what we have endured and achieved, in the peaceful transference of power, and in the reasonableness and moderation of the sovereigns we have elected. But there is also much humility to be learned. We look back with amazement at the ignorance and moral obtuseness revealed by what our past leaders have said and our past citizens believed. We should recognize that 50 or 100 years from now, readers will shake their heads at what we are saying and believing today.

The conversion of ancient scrolls to crystal memory has made this comparative study possible. Through techniques unknown to our ancestors, we can now experience these decrees not just as text but as living memories, preserved with all their original emotional resonance. This advancement serves historical understanding, allowing us to see patterns across centuries that would otherwise remain hidden.

The decree of Sovereign Helena Mercer provides an instructive case. Archives show she initially drafted a classical-style address, complete with references to ancient philosophy and complex rhetorical structures. Her Vision Pool advisor convinced her to revise it entirely. "Your words must move not the mind alone but the spirit," the advisor wrote. "When a mother in Eastridge holds her sick child and hears you speak of health reforms, she needs not elegant allusions but the conviction that her sovereign understands her suffering and calls her to hope." Mercer's final decree contained twenty-three instances of "Let us..."—direct appeals to citizen action rather than descriptions of policy.

As we approach the 54th decree, we would do well to remember this history. The challenges we face—from genetic engineering of magical creatures to the ethical implications of new enchantments—are not entirely new. They echo concerns our ancestors grappled with, though in different forms. The question of how to balance individual liberty with collective good, how to address historical injustices while moving forward, how to preserve our realm's essence while adapting to change—these are eternal questions, asked differently by each generation.

The decrees show us that progress is neither linear nor inevitable. Gains can be lost, wisdom forgotten, moral clarity clouded. But they also show us resilience, the capacity for self-correction, and the power of articulated ideals to eventually reshape reality. In reading them, we commune with our ancestors not as superior descendants but as fellow travelers, struggling with similar questions, limited by our own blind spots as they were by theirs.

May the 54th decree, and all those that follow, be written with awareness of this history, with humility about our own limitations, and with determination to speak truths that future generations will not have to read with shame.
